reading.name: IELTS Reading
reading.description: 60 minutes, 40 questions across 3 passages. Tests ability to understand main ideas, details, inferences, and writer's attitudes in academic texts.

kcs.name: Understanding Main Ideas
kcs.description: Identifying the primary argument, theme, or purpose of a passage or paragraph. Understanding what the writer is trying to convey overall, not just individual facts.
commonErrors: Confusing a supporting detail with the main idea — the detail is evidence, not the point
Selecting the first sentence as the main idea when the main idea appears later in the paragraph
Choosing an answer that is too broad (beyond scope of passage) or too narrow (only covers one paragraph)
Missing the writer's overall argument because of focus on individual words
exerciseTemplates: Match each paragraph to its main idea from a list of headings
Read a paragraph and write one sentence summarizing it, then compare to model answer
For a given passage, identify which sentence in each paragraph states the main idea

kcs.name: Locating Specific Details
kcs.description: Finding and understanding specific facts, numbers, dates, names, or pieces of information explicitly stated in the passage. The answer is directly present in the text — no inference needed.
commonErrors: Scanning for exact keywords instead of paraphrased equivalents (e.g., searching for 'building' when passage says 'structure')
Selecting information from the wrong paragraph because a keyword appears in multiple places
Missing the answer because it's embedded in a complex sentence structure
Reading too slowly — trying to understand every word instead of scanning strategically
exerciseTemplates: Timed scanning drill: find 5 specific pieces of information in 2 minutes
Paraphrase matching: match 10 statements to their paraphrased equivalents in the passage
Short-answer questions based on explicitly stated facts

kcs.name: Making Inferences
kcs.description: Reading between the lines — understanding what is implied but not directly stated. Distinguishing between what the passage explicitly says, what it suggests, and what is not mentioned at all. This is the foundation for T/F/NG and Y/N/NG question types.
commonErrors: Assuming information that is not stated — treating common knowledge or personal opinion as if it's in the passage
Confusing implication with direct statement — 'the passage suggests X' is different from 'the passage says X'
Failing to distinguish between FALSE (passage says the opposite) and NOT GIVEN (passage doesn't mention it at all)
Over-inferring — drawing conclusions that go beyond what the text reasonably supports
exerciseTemplates: For each statement, classify as STATED, IMPLIED, or NOT MENTIONED based on a short passage
Given a passage and 5 inferences, identify which are supported and which are not, with evidence
Read a paragraph and write 2 valid inferences and 2 invalid inferences

kcs.name: True / False / Not Given
kcs.description: Evaluating whether factual statements agree with (TRUE), contradict (FALSE), or are not mentioned in (NOT GIVEN) the passage. The most distinctive and challenging IELTS Reading question type. Tests the ability to distinguish what the passage confirms, what it denies, and what it simply doesn't address.
commonErrors: Selecting NOT GIVEN when the passage implies FALSE — the single most common error. If the passage says 'X causes Y' and the statement says 'X prevents Y', the answer is FALSE, not NOT GIVEN
Selecting FALSE when the passage mentions something similar but not contradictory — similar ≠ contradictory
Selecting TRUE when only part of the statement is supported — the ENTIRE statement must be true
Overthinking NOT GIVEN — if you can't find any mention after careful search, it IS NOT GIVEN
Letting personal knowledge influence the answer — IELTS tests passage comprehension, not general knowledge
exerciseTemplates: 5-question T/F/NG set based on a short academic passage
Single-statement classification drill: 10 rapid-fire T/F/NG decisions with immediate feedback
Error analysis: given 5 incorrect T/F/NG answers with the passage, explain why each answer is wrong
Compare-and-contrast: same passage, identify 2 TRUE statements, 2 FALSE statements, and 2 NOT GIVEN statements

kcs.name: Yes / No / Not Given
kcs.description: Evaluating whether statements about the writer's views, opinions, or claims agree with (YES), contradict (NO), or are not expressed in (NOT GIVEN) the passage. Unlike T/F/NG which deals with facts, Y/N/NG deals with the writer's opinions and claims.
commonErrors: Treating Y/N/NG as identical to T/F/NG — mixing up fact-based and opinion-based evaluation
Attributing a commonly-held opinion to the writer when the writer doesn't express it
Confusing the writer's report of someone else's view with the writer's own view
Missing hedging language ('may', 'could', 'perhaps') that weakens a claim
exerciseTemplates: 5-question Y/N/NG set based on an argumentative passage
Writer's view identification: highlight sentences that express the writer's opinion vs. reported facts
Contrast drill: same statements against both T/F/NG and Y/N/NG rubrics — understand the difference

kcs.name: Multiple Choice
kcs.description: Selecting the correct answer from 4 options (A-D). Tests ability to understand detailed meaning, identify the writer's purpose, or choose the best title. Distractors are designed to be plausible — often containing words from the passage used in misleading ways.
commonErrors: Choosing the first plausible-sounding answer without checking all four options
Selecting an option that uses exact words from the passage but changes the meaning (word-matching trap)
Picking an option that is true in general but doesn't answer the specific question asked
Being distracted by an option that sounds academic or complex but is factually wrong
Running out of time because of over-analyzing each option
exerciseTemplates: 5-question multiple choice set with detailed feedback explaining why each distractor is wrong
Distractor analysis: for each wrong option, explain what makes it tempting and why it's incorrect
Timed MC drill: 10 questions in 15 minutes, then review accuracy vs speed

kcs.name: Gap-Fill & Sentence Completion
kcs.description: Completing sentences, summaries, notes, tables, or diagrams by filling gaps with words from the passage. Tests ability to locate specific information and understand paraphrased relationships. Word limit is strictly enforced (e.g., NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS).
commonErrors: Exceeding the word limit — writing 3 words when the instruction says NO MORE THAN TWO
Spelling errors — misspelled words are marked wrong even if the intended word is correct
Using words not from the passage — all answers must come directly from the text
Copying surrounding words incorrectly — paying attention to grammar (singular/plural, tense)
Missing the answer because the gap in the question uses different wording than the passage
exerciseTemplates: 5-question gap-fill based on a passage excerpt with strict word limit enforcement
Summary completion: fill 8 gaps in a passage summary using words from the original text
Paraphrase matching warm-up: match gapped sentences to the original passage sentences

kcs.name: Matching Headings & Information
kcs.description: Matching headings to paragraphs (identifying the main theme of each paragraph) or matching specific pieces of information to the paragraph that contains them. Tests both global understanding (headings) and detailed search (information matching). There are always more headings than paragraphs.
commonErrors: Matching based on a single shared keyword rather than the overall meaning of the paragraph
Getting stuck on one difficult match and running out of time for the remaining questions
Not eliminating used headings — wasting time re-reading options already matched
For information matching: searching for exact words instead of paraphrased ideas
Matching a heading that covers only the first sentence, not the whole paragraph
exerciseTemplates: Matching headings: 6 paragraphs, 8 headings — match each paragraph to the best heading
Information matching: locate which paragraph (A-F) contains each of 5 specific pieces of information
Strategy drill: read only the first and last sentence of each paragraph, attempt heading matching, then verify with full reading

kcs.name: Vocabulary in Context
kcs.description: Determining the meaning of unfamiliar words from the surrounding context. IELTS passages contain academic vocabulary — test-takers are not expected to know every word but must use context clues (surrounding sentences, examples, contrast signals) to infer meaning.
commonErrors: Choosing the most common dictionary definition rather than the meaning that fits the context
Ignoring contrast signals ('however', 'although', 'rather than') that indicate the word means the opposite of what's expected
Not using the surrounding 2-3 sentences to build context — focusing only on the sentence containing the word
Giving up on a word too quickly — many difficult words are explained or exemplified in the following sentences
exerciseTemplates: Context clues drill: given 5 sentences with unfamiliar words, select the correct meaning from 4 options
Word-in-context: read a paragraph, identify 3 challenging words, and define them using only passage context
Contrast signal practice: identify contrast words (however, yet, although) and what they reveal about surrounding vocabulary

listening.name: IELTS Listening
listening.description: 30 minutes, 40 questions across 4 sections. KCs will be defined in Phase 2.

writing.name: IELTS Writing
writing.description: 60 minutes, 2 tasks (Task 1: 150+ words describing a graph/chart/diagram, Task 2: 250+ words essay). Scored across 4 rubric criteria: Task Response (TR), Coherence & Cohesion (CC), Lexical Resource (LR), Grammatical Range & Accuracy (GRA). Unlike Reading, errorRate is derived from band gap between current and target band, not from right/wrong counts.

kcs.name: Task Response (TR)
kcs.description: How fully and appropriately the candidate addresses the task. Task 1: identifies key features, supports with data, provides overview. Task 2: presents a clear position, develops main ideas with supporting evidence, addresses all parts of the question. The most heavily weighted criterion in determining the overall Writing band.
commonErrors: Task 1: listing every data point without identifying key trends or providing an overview paragraph
Task 2: going off-topic or addressing only part of the question — e.g., discussing advantages but forgetting disadvantages
Task 2: stating opinions without supporting them with specific examples or evidence
Task 1: writing under the minimum word count (150 words) — examiner penalizes this directly
Task 2: giving a balanced discussion when the question asks 'To what extent do you agree or disagree?' — must take a clear position
exerciseTemplates: Given a Task 2 question, write a position statement and 3 main ideas with one supporting example each — Claude checks if they address all parts of the question
Task 1 overview drill: given 3 different graphs, write only the overview paragraph (2-3 sentences) identifying the main trend
Paragraph purpose check: read a sample essay paragraph-by-paragraph and identify what each paragraph contributes to answering the question
kcs.scoringNote: errorRate for Writing is computed from band gap: gap = (targetBand - currentBand) / targetBand. A gap of 0.5 bands on a 7.0 target = errorRate of 0.07. ErrorRate accumulates across multiple writing submissions.

kcs.name: Coherence & Cohesion (CC)
kcs.description: How logically the ideas are organized and connected. Includes: paragraph structure (one main idea per paragraph), logical progression of ideas, cohesive devices (linking words, referencing, substitution). Not just 'uses linking words' — overuse of connectors (However, Moreover, Furthermore) actually reduces the score.
commonErrors: Overusing basic connectors at the start of every sentence — 'Firstly... Secondly... Moreover... However... In conclusion...' — this reads as mechanical, not natural
Paragraphs with multiple unrelated ideas jumbled together — one paragraph should develop ONE main point
Missing logical flow between paragraphs — ideas jump from topic to topic without transition
Using referencing incorrectly — 'this', 'these', 'it' pointing to unclear antecedents
Writing paragraphs that are too short (1-2 sentences) or too long (10+ sentences without a clear focus)
exerciseTemplates: Paragraph reordering: given 5 jumbled sentences, arrange them into a logical paragraph — then add one transition sentence to the next paragraph
Connector audit: read a sample essay and replace mechanical connectors with natural referencing ('this approach', 'such policies', 'these developments')
Structure outline: given a Task 2 question, write only the topic sentence for each paragraph — Claude checks logical progression
kcs.scoringNote: CC is graded holistically per essay. errorRate derived from Claude's CC band assessment vs target.

kcs.name: Lexical Resource (LR)
kcs.description: The range, accuracy, and appropriateness of vocabulary used. Includes: use of less common vocabulary, collocations (word partnerships), paraphrasing ability, spelling accuracy, word form precision. High-scoring essays use precise vocabulary and avoid repetition through paraphrasing.
commonErrors: Repeating the same basic words throughout the essay — 'important' used 6 times instead of varying with 'significant', 'crucial', 'essential', 'vital'
Using 'big words' incorrectly to sound impressive — a word used in the wrong context damages the score more than a simple word used correctly
Spelling errors on common IELTS vocabulary — 'accommodation', 'government', 'environment', 'nowadays'
Writing phrases that are grammatically correct but unnatural in English — direct translations from native language
Not using collocations — writing 'make a decision' as 'do a decision', 'heavy rain' as 'strong rain'
exerciseTemplates: Paraphrase drill: rewrite 5 sentences from a sample essay using different vocabulary while preserving meaning — Claude checks accuracy and naturalness
Collocation gap-fill: 10 sentences with missing collocations — select from word pairs like 'make/do', 'heavy/strong', 'high/tall'
Vocabulary upgrade: given a Band 5.0 paragraph, replace underlined words with higher-level alternatives — Claude shows a Band 7.0 version
kcs.scoringNote: LR benefits from vocabulary tracking in student profile (misspelledWords, weakTopics). Cross-references with reading vocabulary work.

kcs.name: Grammatical Range & Accuracy (GRA)
kcs.description: The variety and correctness of sentence structures used. Includes: range of sentence types (simple, compound, complex), error density (how many errors per 100 words), error severity (do errors impede communication?), and punctuation accuracy. High bands require a mix of structures with few errors.
commonErrors: Writing only simple sentences — 'subject + verb + object' pattern repeated throughout, no complex structures
Frequent subject-verb agreement errors — 'the number of people are increasing' instead of 'is increasing'
Inconsistent verb tense within a paragraph — switching between past and present without reason
Article errors — missing 'a/an/the' or using them incorrectly (the most common error for non-native speakers)
Comma splices — joining two complete sentences with only a comma instead of using a period, semicolon, or conjunction
exerciseTemplates: Sentence combining: given 3 simple sentences, combine them into one grammatically correct complex sentence — Claude checks accuracy
Error correction: given a paragraph with 10 grammatical errors, identify and correct each one
Structure variety check: analyze your own essay — count simple vs compound vs complex sentences. Target: at least 40% complex

kcs.name: Article Usage (a/an/the)
kcs.description: Correct use of definite article (the), indefinite articles (a/an), and zero article. The most persistent error pattern for learners from languages without article systems (Chinese, Vietnamese, Japanese, Korean). Mastery requires understanding: specificity (the = known to reader), generality (a/an = one of many, zero article = general concept).
commonErrors: Omitting 'the' before a specific noun already mentioned — 'I visited museum. Museum was crowded.'
Using 'the' with general plural nouns — 'The dogs are loyal animals' when meaning dogs in general
Confusing 'a' and 'an' based on spelling not sound — 'a hour' instead of 'an hour', 'an university' instead of 'a university'
Missing articles before singular countable nouns — 'He is teacher' instead of 'He is a teacher'
Overusing 'the' with abstract concepts — 'The happiness is important' instead of 'Happiness is important'
exerciseTemplates: Article gap-fill: 15 sentences with blanks where articles should go — fill in a/an/the or leave blank for zero article
Error detection: given a paragraph, circle every article error and explain the rule that was broken
Pattern drill: write 5 sentences about a specific topic, then rewrite them as general statements — observe how articles change

kcs.name: Verb Tense Consistency
kcs.description: Accurate and consistent use of verb tenses within and across sentences. Includes: present/past/future distinction, perfect tenses (have done, had done), conditional forms, and tense agreement in complex sentences. Task 1 especially tests tense control — describing a graph showing past data requires consistent past tense.
commonErrors: Switching between past and present tense mid-paragraph when describing the same data — 'The graph showed... it shows... the figures increased...'
Using present perfect incorrectly for completed past actions — 'I have visited Paris in 2019' instead of 'I visited Paris in 2019'
Forgetting to use past perfect for the earlier of two past events — 'By the time I arrived, the train left' instead of 'had left'
Using 'will' in if-clauses — 'If it will rain, I will stay home' instead of 'If it rains, I will stay home'
Task 1: describing a future projection with past tense — confusing forecast data with historical data
exerciseTemplates: Tense correction: given a paragraph with 8 verb tense errors, correct each one and explain the time relationship
Timeline writing: given a sequence of events on a timeline, write a paragraph using appropriate tenses — Claude checks consistency
Task 1 tense drill: given 3 graphs (past data, current comparison, future projection), write 2 sentences for each using the correct tense

kcs.name: Complex Sentence Structures
kcs.description: Ability to use a variety of sentence structures beyond simple sentences. Includes: subordinate clauses (although, while, because, which), conditional sentences (if/then, unless), relative clauses (who, that, where), passive voice for academic register, and nominalization (turning verbs into nouns for formal style). High bands require accurate use of complex structures, not just attempts.
commonErrors: Attempting complex sentences but creating fragments — subordinate clause left alone as if it were a complete sentence
Overcomplicating sentences to the point of confusion — a 40-word sentence that the reader must re-read to understand
Using the wrong relative pronoun — 'The city which I was born' instead of 'The city where I was born'
Avoiding passive voice entirely — academic writing requires some passive constructions ('The experiment was conducted' not 'They conducted the experiment')
Writing only 'although' and 'because' sentences — never using 'despite', 'whereas', 'while', 'unless', 'provided that'
exerciseTemplates: Structure transformation: rewrite 5 simple sentences as complex sentences using different structures — Claude checks grammatical accuracy
Sentence deconstruction: take a 35-word Band 9 sentence, break it into its component clauses — understand how it's built
Pattern practice: write 3 sentences each using: although/while, if/unless, a relative clause, and passive voice

speaking.name: IELTS Speaking
speaking.description: 11-14 minutes, 3 parts. KCs will be defined in Phase 2 after Reading/Listening KCs are validated.
